content:
Amazon is trying to enlist New York City customers to join its fight against a city council bill challenging the retail giant’s controversial delivery model.

On Thursday, New York-based Amazon shoppers who went to the company’s website or app were greeted by a warning that said “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” The message — with a red “attention” banner at top — was a reference to the Delivery Protection Act, a bill that would require Amazon to directly hire the drivers who deliver its packages in the city.

Customers who clicked on the link were encouraged to reach out to their council members about legislation that “could increase prices for New Yorkers,” and were invited to provide their names and contact information. They also received a message urging them to “act now to protect low prices” at checkout.

The move marks an escalation in Amazon’s fight with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other Democratic backers of the bill, who say it will improve working conditions for delivery drivers and make the city’s streets safer.

In a post to X addressing the messages, Mamdani noted that Amazon is a “multi-trillion dollar company.”

“If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council’s efforts to protect workers’ rights and keep our streets safe. It’s greed,” the mayor said.

Amazon said its prompt had led to 60,000 emails being sent to the council as of Friday afternoon.

“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written — which is why we’re doing this,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement. “If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill.”

Amazon’s effort to mobilize its customer base against the legislation is not a surprise, given the stakes.

Although it now delivers more parcels than UPS, Amazon outsources most of its delivery work to smaller, little-known firms it calls “delivery service partners.” Amazon drivers are technically employed by the DSPs, even though they wear Amazon uniforms, work out of Amazon facilities and deliver Amazon packages.

Amazon defends the system and claims it helps grow small businesses, but critics including unions, labor academics and the Mamdani administration argue it drives down working conditions and helps Amazon avoid legal liabilities and labor standards.

The Delivery Protection Act would blow a hole in Amazon’s DSP system by forcing the company to employ drivers directly if it wants to deliver packages out of city facilities. It would also shake up FedEx and other logistics companies that rely on a similar model.

The International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which represents UPS drivers, is among the biggest backers of the legislation. The union has struggled to organize Amazon’s drivers in part because the DSP system makes the workforce more fragmented.

Julie Su, New York’s deputy mayor for economic justice, told HuffPost in September that such outsourcing had “proliferated across the economy” and made jobs “more precarious and less secure for working people.” She said the direct-hire mandate was meant to make companies like Amazon more accountable, including for driver safety.

“We cannot hide from the fact that some corporations are so large and influential that their business practices impact entire industries,” Su said.

Amazon has warned that if the legislation passes, it would put its DSPs out of business. The company has threatened to pull its delivery hubs out of New York City, which would require drivers to pick parcels up in New Jersey and Connecticut, leading to longer delivery times for customers.

The company said its estimate that the bill could add $5 to each delivery came from an analysis done by a consulting group for the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a business coalition that’s received funding from Amazon and has been airing advertisements against the bill.

Nantel said the company is “hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written.” She added that Amazon has invited council members to visit its delivery hubs and talk to DSP owners but hasn’t gotten many takers.

“We continue urging them to do so, and hope they’ll be willing to work with us,” she said.
